title: Start seedlings under gentler light
author: Maya
body: Seedlings burn easily under full-strength LED or HPS. Run lower intensity (or raise the light higher) for the first 1–2 weeks, then step up as true leaves develop. Photoperiod plants generally want 18/6 light during veg and 12/12 to trigger flowering.

title: Watch for nutrient burn before you chase deficiencies
author: Chris
body: Start new nutrient lines at half the bottle's recommended strength and work up. Dark, crispy leaf tips usually mean too much nitrogen, not too little — it's easy to overcorrect in the wrong direction.

title: Check the underside of leaves weekly
author: Jordan
body: Spider mites and aphids show up on the underside of leaves long before you notice damage up top. Catch them early with neem oil, and keep airflow moving through the canopy to head off powdery mildew.

title: Low-stress training builds an even canopy
author: Priya
body: Gently bending and tying down branches early in veg (instead of topping) spreads the canopy out so more bud sites get direct light — usually a bigger yield bump than people expect from such a low-effort technique.

title: Trichomes tell you when to harvest — not pistil hairs
author: Sam
body: Use a jeweler's loupe on the trichomes, not the color of the hairs. Mostly cloudy trichomes with a few amber ones is peak THC; more amber shifts the effect milder and sleepier. Cure in glass jars afterward, burping daily for the first week or two.

title: Feminized vs. autoflower seeds for beginners
author: Maya
body: Feminized photoperiod seeds give you control over veg length and usually a bigger final yield. Autoflowers finish faster on their own schedule and are more forgiving of light-schedule mistakes — a solid pick for a first grow.

title: Dial in airflow and odor control before you plant
author: Chris
body: An oscillating fan, a carbon filter, and slight negative pressure in the tent solve most mold and smell problems before they start — much easier than fixing them mid-grow.

title: Time outdoor planting to your local frost date
author: Jordan
body: Photoperiod plants outdoors start flowering as days shorten in late summer, so know your area's first frost date before you commit to a strain's flowering time. In humid climates, mold-resistant strains save a lot of heartbreak late in the season.
